newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ to crusade in China against plunging wool sales.
newsitem.headline: NZ to crusade in China against plunging wool sales.

text.p: Wools of New Zealand said on Friday it was planning a new crusade in China, its most important market, to counter a plunge in sales.

"The issues are complex and we can't restore prices and quality overnight, but I am optimistic about the opportunities to rebuild New Zealand's image in China," chief executive Jeff Jackson said on his return from a week-long crisis fact-finding trip to China.
"We plan to run a quality and product development crusade in China," he added.

China and Hong Kong imported NZ$390 million, 39 percent of of New Zealand's clip in the June 1996 year, down from $442 million the previous year. Sales for the nine months to March 31, 1997 were $198 million.
Although not prepared to speculate on the short-term demand, Jackson said the substantial drop in shipments in the early months of the year did not indicate a longer-term demand level.
The sales plunge was due to high product stock levels held by Chinese state-owned mills in particular, he said.
"These will work themselves through the system and we should return to a more even keel in a few months," he said.

Some leading New Zealand exporters have suggested the fall in sales to China was a long-term phenomenon as China switched away from New Zealand's coarser wools suitable for hard-yarn and carpets to finer merino-type wools used for worsted production.
Jackson said increasing privatisation in China had caused "an excessively competitive market" driving down prices and quality.
The increasing importance of the private sector in China and the financial difficulties of the state-owned enterprises was changing the landscape of wool usage in China.
"The influences of the old command economy are still there but increasingly the private sector is in the driving sector."
Chinese processors Jackson met in China had complained about the quality of New Zealand wool.

"There are now hundreds of Chinese wool importers who are just traders. The problem is that in a newly deregulated economy, most them know nothing about wool but know all about driving a hard bargain," Jackson said.
And New Zealand importers were compromising quality to make a sale. Jackson acknowledged the declining reputation of New Zealand wool was serious.
But encouragingly, he said, the processing sector in China was striking back by demanding deliveries true to description.
"Some at least are now prepared to pay the premium required by those exporters seeking to preserve their reputation in this crucial market."
Jackson said New Zealand would capitalise on the trend towards softer and more sophisticated apparel products and Wools of New Zealand would support the development of the carpet market.
"The issues are complex and we can't restore prices and quality overnight, but I am optimistic about the opportunities to re-build New Zealand's image in China," Jackson said.
